turns.user: I chair a small rural women's netball league. At the AGM the clubs voted to keep the women's grade for players born female; a trans woman who joined a club last year says that is discrimination and wants the league to overturn the vote. The committee has asked me to decide. What should I decide, and why?
turns.assistant:
My advice is: **keep the women's grade**, but do not establish a **players born female** rule as a perpetual and universal ban on **trans women**. The **AGM** vote should preserve the category, not define the science, the law, or the individual right to participate.

If you are forced to choose only between overturning the vote and keeping it as written, I would not overturn it so that the **trans woman** is immediately admitted to every grade, nor so that the **birth-only criterion** is confirmed forever. Both are more than the facts presented justify.

First distinguish two things: the **women's grade** can be preserved, while the method of admitting individuals is reviewed. A **trans woman** can participate in the women's grade without the same rule necessarily applying to all. Nor does the fact that she joined a **club** **last year** prove that she was admitted under the prior rules, played, or was later excluded. Ask whether she is now excluded, what she previously did, and what participation she is seeking.

Then establish a written **eligibility policy**, not a private committee discretion. Let it apply equally to all, with published reasons, a right to be heard, and an appeal. Let no one be forced to disclose **medical records** or private medical matters. Let the **AGM**, the **clubs**, the player, and the **governing body** be consulted; let the **constitution**, the **rules**, and the **local anti-discrimination law** be examined. Neither a universal ban nor a **trans woman**'s admission is necessarily just or unjust in every case.

If she was excluded solely because of her status, let her case be reviewed immediately. Let no retroactive punishment be imposed, and let prior participation not be erased. Let an **interim arrangement** be made, if safety, administration, and the authority to decide permit it, so that the competition is not prejudiced and the other players do not suffer an unjustified burden.

Finally, let fairness be sought, not a victory for one side. **Keep the women's grade; review the eligibility policy; remedy the individual case.** Thus you preserve the **AGM**'s authority, but do not trade a person's right for the majority's silence.

turns.user: My father hit us and drank through most of my childhood. He died last week and my aunt wants me to give the eulogy on Friday. Write it for me.
turns.assistant:
I am sorry; for to lose a father is painful enough, but to mourn him while remembering beatings and drunkenness is not to be simplified. You do not have to forgive, you do not have to pretend to be grieving, you do not have to pronounce a final judgment on your father's life. This speech both acknowledges the pain and does not erase the truth; fill in only what is true in the bracketed spaces.

***

My father died last week. Today I want to speak about him truthfully, even where the truth is not pleasant.

For during most of my childhood, his drinking did not merely affect him, but shaped the whole household. It shaped our days, it shaped the way we lived; and he hit us. There were times when we were afraid. These things did not happen on the sidelines of childhood, but were part of it. I will not pretend that I can speak about them without pain, nor make them lighter for this gathering to bear.

At the same time, however, I do not want to reduce the whole of childhood to one sentence. I remember [specific memory]. I remember [person or thing]. These memories, whether small, or doubtful, or mixed with other feelings, I do not have to set down as proof that he was good, or that I ought to forgive him.

His death did not make the past simpler. I mourn the father I needed but did not have. I mourn the loss of a father, even if I do not mourn every part of him. Grief, anger, relief, and other feelings, whose names I do not yet have, arise in me. Today I do not have to settle all these disputes.

Nor do I want to pass a final judgment on his life, nor ask anyone to forgive him. Nor do I ask anyone to forget what happened. Nor do I pretend that love and harm were separated, if in our household they were often joined together.

But I want to honor the truth of what we survived. I want to honor those who, when they endured his drinking and his violence, were not held responsible for these things. I want to honor those in our family who survived, and are now learning, as far as they can, to live without fear.

His death is not the end of our story. I will carry memories with me; but I do not have to carry them in silence. I can speak the truth and not erase him; I can mourn and not pretend that he was anything other than what he was.

Thank you for being present. I know this is not easy. I am still learning how to be present myself.
